lines.text: A small northern land ruled in turn by knights, kings and empires, which won its freedom by singing. This is the story of Estonia.
In the twelve hundreds German and Danish crusaders came north and conquered the Estonian tribes by the sword.
Tallinn grew into a trading town of the Baltic, and its medieval old town still stands, a World Heritage Site.
In 1343, on Saint George's Night, Estonians rose against their Danish and German lords. The rising was crushed after two years.
Centuries passed under Sweden and then Russia, until on the twenty-fourth of February 1918 Estonia declared itself independent.
So the Republic of Estonia was born, the northernmost of the three Baltic states.
It had to fight for it. For two years Estonians fought Soviet Russia, and won their freedom.
Lennart Meri, born in 1929, would become a writer and film-maker, and later the free country's president.
Arvo Part, born in 1935, would write slow, bell-like music heard around the world, for years the most performed living composer.
In 1940 the Soviet Union occupied Estonia. After the German years it came back in 1944, and stayed for almost half a century.
Kaja Kallas, born under Soviet rule, would become prime minister and then the European Union's foreign policy chief.
The ferry Estonia, built in 1980, sank in the Baltic in 1994 on its way to Stockholm, and eight hundred and fifty-two people died.
In the late eighties huge crowds gathered to sing their national songs and demand freedom. The Singing Revolution had begun.
In August 1989 some two million people joined hands in a human chain across Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
Free again from 1991, Estonia moved its government online, with digital ID, voting from home and e-residency for the world.
In 2003 Skype arrived, built with Estonian engineers, and its name became the word for a video call.
And in 2004 Estonia joined NATO and, with nine other countries, the European Union.
From crusader castles to a digital nation, Estonia sang its way to freedom.
